cumbia.name: Cumbia
cumbia.description: Born on Colombia's Caribbean coast, cumbia has travelled all over Latin America (Mexico, Peru, Argentina…). Its engine: the guacharaca (the guiro) going "chaa-k-k" on every beat, a bass alternating root and fifth, and accents on the off-beats that get the hips swaying.

son.name: Son cubano
son.description: The ancestor of salsa. Everything is built around the clave, a 5-stroke pattern over 2 bars (here "3-2": three strokes, then two). The "tumbao" bass plays ahead, on the & of 2 and on 4: it anticipates the next chord.

bossa.name: Bossa nova
bossa.description: Born in Rio in the late 1950s, bossa nova is a slowed-down, intimate samba. The guitar plays two roles at once: the thumb plays the bass on beats 1 and 3, while the fingers pinch the chords off the beat, like the "rim" pattern (the rim of the snare drum).

reggaeton.name: Reggaeton
reggaeton.description: Reggaeton is built on the "dembow": kick drum on every beat and snare in 3+3+2 ("boom-chick… boom-chick"). Being so steady, it's an excellent style for working on precision.

chachacha.name: Cha-cha-chá
chachacha.description: Invented in Havana in the 1950s by Enrique Jorrín, the cha-cha-chá is named after the sound of the dancers' feet on "4-&-1". The güiro plays three long scrapes then two short ones ("chaa, chaa, chaa, cha-cha"), and the cowbell marks every beat.

bolero.name: Bolero
bolero.description: The romantic ballad of Latin America, born in Cuba and adopted by Mexican guitar trios. Slow tempo, bongos rolling in eighth notes (the "martillo"), bass settled on 1 and 3: the ideal style for polishing your chord changes without being rushed.

foxtrot.name: Guinguette foxtrot
foxtrot.description: Arriving from the United States in the 1920s, the foxtrot became a pillar of the musette dance halls and the riverside guinguettes along the Marne, with accordion, banjo and double bass. Its engine: the "pompe" (boom-chick) — bass on 1 and 3, chord slapped on 2 and 4 ("boom-chak"). Played fast, it's one of the most infectious rhythms there is.

swing.name: Swing
swing.description: In swing, eighth notes aren't even: the first is long, the second short ("doo-ba, doo-ba"). That lilt is what makes the jazz of the 1930s, and the gypsy jazz of Django Reinhardt, king of the guinguettes. The double bass "walks" on every beat, and the cymbal goes "ding, ding-a-ding".

rumba.name: Flamenco rumba
rumba.description: Born where flamenco met the Cuban rumba, the rumba flamenca is flamenco's most festive rhythm (the one the Gipsy Kings made famous). The cajón hits the bass on 1 and 3 and slaps on 2 and 4, the palmas clap "a contratiempo" on the off-beats, and the guitar alternates strums and muted hits.

tangos.name: Flamenco tangos
tangos.description: Nothing to do with the Argentine tango: flamenco tangos are an energetic, danceable 4-beat compás. Their signature: the palmas stay silent on beat 1 and clap 2, 3, 4. The guitar "fills" that first beat. Rumba is their lighter cousin.

sevillanas.name: Sevillanas
sevillanas.description: The folk dance of the Seville Fair, which everyone dances in pairs. A lively 3-beat rhythm with a strong accent on 1. The castanets play a roll ("carretilla") on 1 then two crisp clicks, and the palmas mark every beat.

solea.name: Soleá
solea.description: The "mother" of flamenco, deep and solemn. Its compás is 12 beats long, accented on 3, 6, 8, 10 and 12: you feel it as two groups of 3 (1-2-3, 4-5-6) followed by three groups of 2 (7-8, 9-10, 11-12). Flamenco musicians often count from 12; here we start from 1 to keep it simple.

alegrias.name: Alegrías
alegrias.description: The same 12-beat compás as soleá, but in major, faster and brighter: the song of joy, born in the port of Cádiz. The palmas clap on every off-beat ("a contratiempo") and the guitar changes chords on accents 3 and 10.

bulerias.name: Bulerías
bulerias.description: The 12-beat compás played very fast, with humour and virtuosity: the rhythm of the gitano fiestas of Jerez. The accents stay on 3, 6, 8, 10 and 12, but the palmas and cajón play around them with off-beats. To follow it, you have to feel the accents rather than count every beat.

cumbia-mexicana.name: Mexican cumbia
cumbia-mexicana.description: Arriving from Colombia in the 1950s, cumbia became the music of Mexico's popular dances: accordion-led cumbia norteña, and the cumbia sonidera of the sound systems. More laid-back than the original, it rests on the guiro, a bass alternating root and fifth, and a keyboard stabbing the off-beats.

cumbia-peruana.name: Chicha (Peruvian cumbia)
cumbia-peruana.description: In 1960s-70s Peru, cumbia met psychedelic rock and Andean melodies: that's chicha. The electric guitar sings the melody, a second guitar plays a tight 16th-note "chucu", and the timbales and bongos roll over the guiro.

cumbia-villera.name: Cumbia villera
cumbia-villera.description: Born in the late 1990s in the working-class neighbourhoods ("villas") of Buenos Aires, cumbia villera is faster and rawer: guiro, kick drum on 1 and 3, cracking timbales and a keyboard marking every off-beat.

foxtrot-bal.name: Dance-hall foxtrot (four-beat)
foxtrot-bal.description: The foxtrot as it was played to get people dancing: the double bass walks on all four beats, the kick drum pushes every beat, the piano slaps 2 and 4. Between 180 and 220 bpm it's a steam train: the ukulele (or banjo) has to play tight, short and never slow down.

charleston.name: Charleston
charleston.description: The wild dance of the 1920s: the whole band hits together on 1 and just before 3 ("Charles-ton!"), then leaves a gap. Very fast tempo, 200 bpm and up. For the ukulele it's a precision exercise: short strokes, muted right away, and fearless syncopations.
